title: Dr Sandie Bohin cont., Summary of interview with Lucy Letby

blocks.text: 2 November 2022
Baby C
Housekeeping
DR SANDIE BOHIN (continued)
Examination-in-chief by MR JOHNSON (continued)
Cross-examination by MR MYERS
Re-examination by MR JOHNSON
Questions from THE JUDGE
Summary of interview with LUCY LETBY re [Baby C] (read)
Housekeeping
Wednesday, 2 November 2022
(Delay in proceedings)
(In the absence of the jury)
Housekeeping
My Lord, we're grateful for the additional time this morning. I'd be grateful if I can just raise with you later today, when we've dealt with the evidence, any issues arising. Thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Certainly. We will do, thank you. I'll apologise to the jury but not say anything about why we're late.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: My Lord, yes.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: (In the presence of the jury)
DR SANDIE BOHIN (continued)
Examination-in-chief by MR JOHNSON (continued)
Good morning, members of the jury. My apologies that we weren't ready to start at 10.30.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Circumstances beyond my control. But we're now ready to continue. I apologise for the 20-minute delay.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: My Lord. Just one issue that I didn't deal with yesterday, Dr Bohin.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: The jury heard evidence from Dr Sally Ogden concerning an examination of [Baby C] on 13 June. I'd like to put the page up if we can, please. It's on the iPads. It's page J1922.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: For the record, this, if one were to go back to the previous page, would show that this is an examination conducted by Dr Ogden at 9.30 that morning. So what we can see there on the page is the second page of Dr Ogden's notes.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Towards the bottom of the page -- sorry, the middle of the page, by the second -- where the holes would be if this was a paper sheet, just parallel with where that cross is now, it says -this is an examination, isn't it, that was undertaken by Dr Ogden, as we were told in evidence?
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And on examination, various things are recorded, but the bottom two lines say:
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: "Abdo soft not distended. Bowel sounds heard."
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: So just concentrating on those two lines. In the context of the suggestion that was being put to Dr Gibbs yesterday that potentially [Baby C] had some form of bowel obstruction, what is the relevance of those two findings during the examination by Dr Ogden?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: If a baby had a bowel obstruction, you would expect the abdomen to become distended and also, as part of the examination, it's customary to listen with a stethoscope over the abdomen to listen for bowel sounds. If the abdomen is working normally you can hear what is described as normal bowel sounds, gurgling type sounds.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: If there's an obstruction either there may be no bowel sounds heard because the gut isn't working or there are abnormal, highpitched sounds, classically called tinkling bowel sounds, which would indicate an obstructed bowel.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: The fact that Dr Ogden has written "bowel sounds heard" but has not commented whether they were abnormal and tinkling bowel sounds would lead me to suppose that she has heard bowel sounds and they are normal and therefore the abdomen isn't obstructed.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And therefore, so far as the suggestion that this might be a case where [Baby C]'s bowel was obstructed, what conclusion would you draw?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: From the information that she's written, there is no obstruction.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Thank you. Would you wait there, please, for some further questions?
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Cross-examination by MR MYERS
Dr Bohin, you told the jury yesterday [Baby C] managed really well in the period before his death; is that correct?
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And that's your opinion, is it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: I just want to ask you a little bit about that period first. When I do, keep in mind of course we're not talking about an 8 pound, for instance, full-term baby, are we? He was a very premature baby?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, he was.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And extremely low birth weight?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Probably about the size of a bag of sugar at 800 grams?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Just below that.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And at a high risk of complications?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: He was at risk of complications.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Right. Well, we have your opinion.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I'm going to ask you about some facts about the 24-hour period before his collapse. In fact, he never left intensive care, did he, the intensive care unit?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: He never actually breathed unassisted apart from a couple of hours skin-to-skin contact here or there?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: But he did breathe unassisted when he had several hours of skin-to-skin contact. So yes, he did breathe unassisted.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: I asked you, in fact, he never breathed unassisted apart from a couple of hours to skin-to-skin contact?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's true.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Yes. That was the exception, wasn't it, the couple of hours of skin-to-skin contact?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No. That would be something that would routinely be offered to a baby of any size or gestation if their clinical condition allowed it because there are a great deal of -- a great number of positive benefits to being allowed to have skinto-skin with the mother, both for the mother and the baby. So that would be routine care, not exceptional care.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Can I just confirm, do you agree as a fact that for the majority of his time in intensive care, he never breathed unassisted? The majority of his time.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Well, for -- he wasn't having invasive support apart from very early on in his life when he was intubated.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: So he was receiving respiratory support in the form of CPAP and Optiflow, but that's not assisted breathing, that's respiratory support. He was breathing for himself.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Then do you agree as a fact he never breathed without respiratory support apart from -- or rather for the majority of his time he never breathed without respiratory support?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Within the final 24 hours of his sadly short life, as a fact his CRP, C-reactive protein, was rising, wasn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It had risen before that. It hadn't continued to rise, it had risen to 23.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: To a level that's consistent, as it happens, with infection?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It's consistent with infection or inflammation. That rise to the level of 23 is above normal, which would be about 10, but is not astonishingly high, in the hundreds. It is above normal but you can't tell in isolation whether that's due to an infection or an inflammatory process; you need to take into account other parameters.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: It's a fact that his platelets had fallen well below what would be considered the healthy acceptable level, hadn't they?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: His weight was down to 717 grams, wasn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And feeding, enteral feeding, had not been able to commence, had it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Well, it could have been commenced but they chose not to commence feeding because of the intrauterine growth retardation and the risk of necrotising enterocolitis, so the clinical team chose not to feed him.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: So as a fact his weight was down to 717 grams and he was not being fed?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: As a fact, within those final 24 hours, he vomited black bile at least once, didn't he?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: He vomited once.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: So you agree with me then?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: You said black bile.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: At least once I said, my Lord.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: There's only one record in the nursing notes of a vomit that I can see.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: I said at least once.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Well, once.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Over that 24-hour period he produced black bile consistently, didn't he?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: He did produce bile. I think that needs to be put into context. There are entries where 0.5ml of bile or black bile or green bile, as it's been described, were aspirated from the nasogastric tube. That's a minuscule amount. So 0.5 of a millilitre is a drop or two, really. So he was not producing copious amounts of black bile, he was producing minuscule amounts.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: He's a tiny baby, isn't he?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Do you agree, any amount of black bile should be a worrying consideration?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Any amount of bile, regardless of colour, is something you should take note of in conjunction with the other clinical findings.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Do you not regard that as worrying, a baby producing black bile consistently, in whatever quantity?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I think the quantity is crucially important. 0.5ml is a very small amount and in a child who's otherwise well I would note it, I would examine the child, and wait to see if that volume increased, if there was a change in clinical condition. As it happened, black bile was aspirated on a few occasions. The amount was -- the volume was not increasing at all. So on its own, in isolation, it isn't necessarily a worrying sign.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Is it a normal finding --
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It's not a --
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: -- black bile?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Bile's green. So if someone's describing a black aspirate I would be concerned that this was not in fact bile, this was altered blood because altered blood is black. I have not seen the description black bile before. There are other descriptions in the nursing notes of bile being dark green, which is much more in keeping with the colour of bile.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Are you questioning that the notes say black bile?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I'm questioning what has been recorded may in fact be altered blood.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Let's have a look then. Could we put up, please, page...
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I think we've seen this a lot of times and it says black bile. I think what the witness is saying is she's not challenging the fact that a black substance was aspirated but querying whether it's bile or whether it's altered blood.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: That's correct, my Lord.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And do you agree as a fact that by the time of death, [Baby C] had pneumonia?
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: He did.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: None of those matters showed that he was managing really well, do they?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I think he was managing well.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Those matters looked at do not indicate he was managing really well?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I'm sorry, I disagree. He was managing well. He had stepped down his respiratory support from CPAP to Optiflow. His respiratory rate was stable. His saturations were stable. He managed time off respiratory support to have skin-to-skin with his parents. That is not a child who is deteriorating.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Are any of the factors that I have set out for you there matters for any concern at all in your opinion, Dr Bohin?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: The fact that he had a bilious aspirate needs to be noted, but, as I've previously said, it needs to be noted in the context of the rest of his clinical condition and not in isolation. They would be a concern if the volume was increasing or if he had abdominal distension or if the aspirates were -- if he was vomiting copious amounts, not small amounts.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Do you agree a baby in [Baby C]'s condition requires very careful monitoring in intensive care?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: And he was receiving very careful monitoring.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Do you agree that when we look at the record for the aspirates, Yvonne Griffiths, the band 6 shift leader, appears to have failed to note on it aspirates that she took from [Baby C]?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: That's not acceptable, is it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's poor nursing practice.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Do you agree that when we look at the records of Sophie Ellis, the nurse who describes feeding [Baby C], has failed to record the one feed that he had prior to his collapse?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: She didn't record it, I agree.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And that's not good practice either, is it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No, it's not good practice.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: I'll come to some of what you say about what took place.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: We've got your report of 6 December 2020. At the time that you made that report -- I think it's paragraph 5.19 if you need to look at it -- you may recall this, your view was that [Baby C]'s collapse has no clear cause in your opinion?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And by the time that we come to August 2022, with the joint report that I referred Dr Evans to yesterday --
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: -- again, so far as the collapse on 13 December is concerned, you don't identify any --
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: June.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: I apologise, my Lord. 13 June.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: It's all right, slip of the tongue.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: You don't identify any collapse, any cause for collapse there, do you?
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And yesterday, when you gave evidence, it remained the case, didn't it, that you could identify no cause for his collapse?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I think yesterday I said that there were two possible causes for his collapse -- I beg your pardon, I was thinking of the 12th, excuse me. No, I did say there was no obvious cause of his collapse.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: That's your evidence, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Let me ask you about infection. Your opinion is that infection did not cause death?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Just so I can understand, and the jury can, when you say infection did not cause death, do you mean that that is your opinion weighing it all up or that it's simply not possible that infection could have caused death?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No, that's my opinion. Infection can cause death, but it's my opinion that infection did not cause death in [Baby C].
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Right. So far as his pneumonia is concerned, would it be right to say your view is it could be a contributory factor to death?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No, I think I said yesterday he died with pneumonia, not of pneumonia, but the fact that he had a pneumonia, in my opinion, made him less responsive to resuscitation.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: I just want to be clear. In the report that you made in December 2020, paragraph 5.4, you say:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "Although [Baby C] had pneumonia at the time of his death, I don't think this was the cause of his collapse."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Which is what you said yesterday.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: "Having said that, there is no doubt in my mind that infection was a contributory factor and may have made him less responsive to resuscitation."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: So taking the two things there, the first thing is do you agree, even if it is not the cause, that infection could have been a contributory factor?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It could because it made him less responsive to resuscitation.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Right. So just so I can understand, where you say:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "There is no doubt infection was a contributory factor and may have made him less responsive to resuscitation."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: What you mean is a contributory factor because it may have made him less responsive?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: So does it follow then that whatever caused the collapse, once that happened, the situation was possibly made worse by his pneumonia, in your opinion?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And therefore, it follows, doesn't it, that the collapse could have been caused by something that actually might not have been fatal but for the pneumonia?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I can't say.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Well, if pneumonia did or might have made him less responsive to resuscitation, then it follows without the pneumonia, he might have responded to resuscitation?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It's impossible to say that.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Does that not simply follow from what you have said, Dr Bohin?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I don't think so, no.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: What difference did it make then?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It made him less responsive to resuscitation because one lung had inflammatory signs, he had a pneumonia, and therefore attempts at resuscitation were -- well, as we know, were futile because he had a pneumonia.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: But that follows, doesn't it, that therefore but for the pneumonia, they might not have been futile?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No, it depends on what the cause of the collapse was.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Well, I'm going to suggest if your opinion is as you put it here, that pneumonia may have made him less responsive to resuscitation, then it follows that but for the pneumonia he might have been resuscitated?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Well, I think that depends, absolutely depends, on what the cause of the collapse was, because for instance if he had been -- if there had been a toxin involved then it wouldn't have mattered how much resuscitation he had, it would have been the toxin that would have ultimately led to his death, whether he had pneumonia or not, so I can't say that but for the pneumonia he would have been more responsive.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Are you suggesting there is a toxin involved?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No, I'm not suggesting (overspeaking) giving an example —
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: There is no evidence of any toxin.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I am not suggesting for one moment that there was a toxin. I was using that as an illustration to say why I didn't think but for the pneumonia he would have survived.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: I'm going to suggest that what follows from what you have said is that the fact of death might not even have happened but for the fact he had pneumonia at the time they tried to resuscitate him on your evidence.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I'm afraid I don't agree with that still.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: You've referred to how well he did and what a good sign it was in terms of skin-to-skin contact; yes?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Of course we have to look at the whole picture in assessing how a baby's condition is, don't we?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Of course.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And you have to put all the signs together to see how the baby is doing. That follows in terms of looking for the bad signs as well as the good signs, doesn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Absolutely, yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And it would be important, wouldn't it, not to be lulled into a false sense of security because of some good signs?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: I want to look at a couple of the items we've seen just so I can explore this with you. We saw a nursing note by Nurse Butterworth made at 9.01 on 12 June. That's at page 1940, Mr Murphy. I'm not sure that this is actually in the S numbers, ladies and gentlemen, but we have seen it and we're just going to look briefly if we could.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: This is some time, it seems, during the 12th, maybe in the morning. Just looking down at the bottom part of this note it says about five lines up:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "Abdo appears distended. Soft firm. Not had bowels opened. At this point minimal clear aspirates."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Just pausing there, we know that position on the aspirates changes in the 24 hours that follows, doesn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, there was another episode where there was a clear aspirate later on, but yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: It changes?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: All right:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "Passing urine currently. Therefore remains in situ. SBRs are still not 50. Under treatment line."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Can you just remind us what SBRs is, please?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Serum bilirubin. So that's the chemical name for the marker for jaundice.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: "Has been quite unsettled at times and has required an increase in oxygen when handling as desaturates."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: So at that point, yes, he was able to come out and be handled but it was accompanied by desaturation when that took place, wasn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: The desaturation didn't occur when he was out with his mother being handled. I think further down on that entry, it's clear that the fact that he was on CPAP was causing him discomfort and when handled on CPAP, he was desaturating. When he was out with his mother, the entry -- either that lady's entry or a subsequent entry, suggests that he settled immediately once he was out.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: That's another entry and we're going to come to that shortly. I'm going through these in order.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: But certainly on 12 June, this note at 9 in the morning, it's got it that he is desaturating when being handled, hasn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: That's not something to be ignored, is it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Well, babies will desaturate if you handle them. So as long as he recovers when the handling is stopped, I wouldn't see that as a sign of deterioration at all.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: I would see that as something that is a normal occurrence when you're handling a baby who is receiving an intervention that he doesn't like because he clearly was uncomfortable with the CPAP.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: We know that an abdominal X-ray some hours after this -we'll return to that in a little while, but let's go to the next note I wanted to go, which is the one you were thinking about perhaps, Dr Bohin. That is for 13 June, a note made by 16.19 by Jennifer Williams. It's at slide 69, page 1947.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: There are a lot of entries here. I'm not going to read through all of this. Just in terms of keeping together the picture, we know other things that have been going on in other records at this time. It's timed at 16.19. If we just look at the second line down of the main entry:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "Nursed on CPAP."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It gives the pressures:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "Blood gas at 900."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: So very good:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "However, [Baby C] very unsettled and fractious."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's something to take note of, isn't it, do you agree?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Not especially because he's very good and his observations are normal and his blood gas is good.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: I think the important thing to take note of, and what the nurse is saying, here is that he's unsettled because he dislikes being on the CPAP, but that isn't causing him a clinical deterioration. It's clearly uncomfortable but it's not causing a clinical deterioration.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Carrying on four or five lines down, it says he calmed down with his mum. And (inaudible) lines below that:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "Again discussed with registrar and decided to try Optiflow in view of [Baby C] being so unsettled on CPAP."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Then the Optiflow commences. Do you see that?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Four or five lines down that:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "CBG taken after 2 hours, satisfactory but not quite as good as the previous one."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: The view of nurse dealing with this at the time, the next two lines, is:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "Shown to registrar and repeat at 18.00. Clinically remains stable but aware do not want to push [Baby C]."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Again, indicating a risk of deterioration, doesn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No, it means he's stable on the Optiflow, but the staff need to be mindful and keep a watch on him.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Next paragraph down:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "Continues to have dark bile aspirates."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, do you agree?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: But improving this afternoon.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: But continuing to have them?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, at 0.5ml when they were aspirated, so an absolutely minuscule amount.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: I'm not going to keep on going over the aspirates.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I'm suggesting to you that any amount of dark bile aspirates being produced consistently from this little baby is a worry and you disagree with that?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I do.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Right. Carrying on down:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "NGT on free drainage."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: So that means that it's open from the stomach out to the atmosphere, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's correct, but from this note it's really unclear whether the -- either the -- the nasogastric tube is on free drainage. What isn't clear from this note is whether the orogastric tubes that he'd previously had over the course of the morning, because he'd pulled two of them out because he was so unsettled, whether they were on free drainage as well. That says
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: the nasogastric tube was on free drainage and that was only placed after 1 o'clock when he was put on to Optiflow.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: So it's not -- that note is, I think, ambiguous and it's not clear if his -- whichever tube he had in was on free drainage for the entire day.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: We know that, of course, aspirates were being taken from him over this period later into the 13th, don't we?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: They were, but aspirates are there and not recorded, just the small amounts of --
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: If the nurses are doing their job properly, if the NGT is on free drainage and aspirates are being taken, it's to be hoped that any air gathering in the stomach will be removed from it, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: We don't know whether they have aspirated air because they haven't recorded it.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: But if it is being aspirated and if he does have NGT on free drainage that should assist in removing air from the stomach, shouldn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It would, but as I've said, it's not clear and the note is ambiguous as to whether he was on free drainage for the entire day or only after 1 o'clock when a nasogastric tube was placed because that was on free drainage. It makes no mention of whether the previous tubes were on free drainage.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: "Abdomen full but soft. Slight shine to abdomen but not veiny or over-distended. Bowels not opened."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: At 3 days in, you would expect the bowels to have opened at some point and in some way generally, wouldn't you, Dr Bohin?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Not necessarily because he hadn't been fed.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: You say not necessarily, but generally would you expect that to happen?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Not necessarily. It may have happened, but I wouldn't regard it as a problem if hadn't happened in a baby that had not been fed. In a baby that had been fed, I would consider it a problem.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Substances like meconium can still pass out, can't they, after birth without being fed?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: They may do but not always.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: With you talking about putting the available clues together, there are things, if we look at everything at this point, which might be matters of concern when put together; do you agree with that?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: They might be but I don't think they were.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: It's not any question of you in any way minimising the seriousness of anything in [Baby C]'s condition? May I just ask that, Dr Bohin?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Absolutely not.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Okay. Indications of intestinal obstruction might include dark bile and vomit, mightn't they?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, they might.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: They might include bowel not opening?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And they might include distension of the abdomen without air actually moving along throughout the length of the abdomen?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, they might.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: If we put up, please, slide 77, which is the note of Sally Ogden that we looked at first thing this morning -- sorry, it's in the [Baby C] section, page 1922.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Slide 77, please, Mr Murphy. It's the same part that we looked at this morning, Dr Bohin.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: As for "abdo soft, not distended", even with an obstruction in place, if the stomach is being aspirated and air removed because a tube is on free drainage, that may mean that even if there's a potential to build up, it may not because the air is coming out?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No, I don't agree with that. The nasogastric tubes that a baby of 800 grams -- the size of the nasogastric tube that a baby of 800 grams would have -- the bore of that would be very, very small and so it would not necessarily remove all the air from within the gut.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: So even with a nasogastric tube in like that, a gut could still distend --
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, it might.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: -- on CPAP?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Right. And even though we see notes from the nurses, in the case of [Baby C], talking about removing aspirates, do you agree that that could have removed air that would otherwise accumulate or not?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, it could, and practice from wherever I've worked would suggest that if copious amounts of air is aspirated up a nasogastric tube, the nurses actually record the volume of that air and we haven't actually -- nowhere in the record is there any volume of air.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Additionally, where anyone feels that a baby may have a bowel obstruction, a larger bored nasogastric tube would be placed so that the removal of air is more efficient. So clearly, no one thought to do that, they clearly weren't concerned about the abdomen at that stage.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: But just because they didn't think to do that doesn't mean there wasn't an obstruction, does it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: There were no clinical indicators of obstruction.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Dr Ogden has written the bowel is soft and not distended. She also heard bowel sounds which means that abdomen was functioning, it wasn't obstructed. Babies who have a bowel obstruction may start off producing bilious aspirates, so bile in the aspirate. The bile continues to be produced and then would increase in volume such that the baby then was vomiting bile and the volume would increase, and at no point has this volume increased.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: If we can just break down a couple of things you said there, Dr Bohin, so we're quite clear. You said that if the nurses, the staff, thought there was an obstruction they might put in a bigger tube to assist with air being taken out?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: That requires that they think of or identify an obstruction in the first place, doesn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: If they hadn't thought of that then they're not going to do that?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Correct.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Secondly, so far as nurses aspirating and drawing out air, if they haven't recorded air, we've heard Nurse Griffiths say she didn't, so far as we understand here, air may still have been taken out of the bowel, mightn't it, when [Baby C] was aspirated?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: But I... I can't see why they wouldn't have recorded it. They've recorded the bile they got out, so why would they not record the air if they are making an entry?
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: So good practice would be to record air as well as bile?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, or aspirates, whatever it is, whether it's clear blood or whatever, yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Aspirates, all right, thank you.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Do you agree in principle, if air is being taken out of the stomach of a baby that's on Optiflow or CPAP, if that's happening, then even with an obstruction, it may not distend at that point if it's being taken out?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No, because it won't all come out, so the abdomen would still be distended if you had an obstruction.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: All right then. We've heard the nurses give evidence, of course, that they were taking air out, haven't we?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: We've heard Ms Griffiths say that. I'll return to that in a moment. But before I do, let me ask you about what this says about sounds.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Dr Ogden's note doesn't describe the bowel sounds, does it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And it doesn't say precisely which part of the abdomen they apply to?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I've never recorded which part of the abdomen bowel sounds apply to.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Do you agree, you couldn't diagnose an obstruction of the gut purely from the presence or absence of bowel sounds, could you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Not on that alone, but the absence of bowel sounds would seriously make you consider that there was an obstruction, or tinkling bowel sounds would make you consider there was an obstruction. But on their own those sounds are not diagnostic of an obstruction.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And clinical decisions in patients with possible bowel obstruction should not be based on auscultatory, in other words just hearing, assessments, should they?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Sorry, could you repeat the question?
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Clinical decisions in patients with a possible bowel obstruction, identifying it, should not be based purely on what you can hear?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Rarely in medicine do you base decisions on a single factor. So like with everything else in this case, information has to be taken in the round. So if there were abnormal or absent bowel sounds and you had a distended abdomen or other features, other clinical features, the constellation of those things would make you investigate further. If you weren't concerned by anything then you wouldn't take it further, obviously, because you'd be unconcerned.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: So this is one clue to what the position may be but it can't be decisive, can it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: She hasn't actually written it there, abnormal. And I think if they were abnormal she would have written down that they were either absent, which she hasn't done, or they were abnormal, ie tinkling bowel sounds, which would indicate an obstruction, and she hasn't written that down. So my inference there is that she heard normal bowel sounds.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: So is it your conclusion, as an expert on this, that the expression "bowel sounds heard" means that you can discount utterly, on the basis of that, the possibility of an obstruction in the abdomen somewhere?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: You can't discount utterly, you have to take bowel sounds in conjunction with the rest of the examination.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Could we have a look then, please, at the X-ray at page 1996, Mr Murphy.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: We've seen this now, we've got the radiologist's commentary on it in the page that follows. So this is the bowel. We can go to the commentary, but do you agree from what we see there that it shows marked distension of the stomach and small intestine?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It shows marked distension of the stomach. I can't delineate whether it's the small or large intestine.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: We've seen the radiologist saying small intestine, haven't we?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, the radiologists have said that. I am unable to distinguish between the two.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Well, let's stay with what the radiologist says at the moment and consider this.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: First of all, with what you said about what would happen if a nurse is aspirating, if Yvonne Griffiths was taking air from the stomach, would you expect it to look like this?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: If it's the case that there is this much air in the stomach and the small intestine and that it hasn't moved through into the large intestine, some sort of obstruction would account for that, wouldn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Not necessarily because [Baby C] hadn't had his bowels opened, so air may not go from the stomach down to the rectum.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Within a 24-hour period after birth, you would expect to start seeing air across the length of the stomach, through the small intestine, into the large intestine and down to the rectum, wouldn't you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Not necessarily, no.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: In general, wouldn't you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Not necessarily, no.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Within 48 hours of birth?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Not if a baby hadn't had their bowels opened, no.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Given the pressure that appears to be here in terms of the distension, what explanation do you give for why gas hasn't simply moved from one part of the intestine to the next?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I don't have an explanation.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: One explanation is there's some sort of obstruction, isn't there?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: But he didn't have clinical signs of obstruction, so no, [Baby C] did not have a bowel obstruction. There are no clinical signs of obstruction. You can't make a diagnosis just on the basis of the X-ray, you have to take everything else into consideration.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: I'd just like you to help with this. I've asked you, if it hasn't moved can you explain why it hasn't, and you said, no, you can't. That is the air. Putting aside what you say about other matters, one reason for it not moving would be if something was obstructing it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That is one reason.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And there is no reason that you can identify as to why it would not have moved if it's this distended?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Well, yes, I can, because he was a premature baby who wasn't being fed, so the peristalsis, which is the muscular contraction of the bowel which pushes fluid, feed and therefore faeces along the bowel was not taking place because he wasn't being fed. So that would be the reason why air had not gone further round, I think.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Let me just ask this before I move on from this because I realise I have asked you a little bit on this topic.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Air is going in under some degree of pressure and it can move through the various pipes to the point we see.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Never mind peristalsis. If that air continues to be put in under pressure, you would expect it to continue to move unless something is in the way, wouldn't you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No, not necessarily. He clinically did not have a bowel obstruction, so regardless of the repeating questions, I don't think he had a bowel obstruction and it's not a given that air would reach the rectum.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Are you aware whether the post-mortem findings of the bowel and air in abdomen indicated any abnormality?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Of what?
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: In [Baby C]'s abdominal cavity. Are you aware of whether the post-mortem findings indicated any kind of abnormality at all, Dr Bohin?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I know what it didn't find. There was an issue of the configuration of the large bowel and where that anatomically sat within the abdominal cavity. I think, although I'm not a pathologist, it's a matter for them to decide whether that's an abnormal finding or not.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: I am led to believe that some pathologists believe that's a normally variant and it's not a problem. Other pathologists perceive it to be a problem. But that's a matter for the pathologists.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Something about the way it's positioned, but that's a matter for the pathologists?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: We'll save it for the pathologists then in that case.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Let me just ask this: 12 June, the distension that we've seen on 12 June, the one we're looking at right now.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: In your report of 6 December, you were of the view that we're looking at could either be due to CPAP or excessive air down the nasogastric tube.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Then if we move forwards to shortly before this trial commenced, the report in August of 2022, page M1260, what you say is this, 036, on this X-ray:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "The cause of the gaseous distension of the bowel and gastric dilation was not CPAP belly. The extent of gaseous distension seen on the X-ray of 12 June 2015 is over and above what is seen in infants requiring CPAP."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's what you said, wasn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: You went on to say about this:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "The massive gastric dilation seen on this X-ray was most likely due to deliberate exogenous administration of air via the NGT."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: So drawing those conclusions together, we've been over the fact that so far as 13 June is concerned there is no cause identified?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: But your opinion is that this appears to be the deliberate administration of air down the NGT on 12 June?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Re-examination by MR JOHNSON

Can I just ask you a couple of questions to clarify a couple of issues? You referred this morning to altered blood. It may be a term of art from a medic's perspective, but could you just explain to the jury, please, what altered blood is?
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, apologies, I should have explained that.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: When blood has been out of a blood vessel for some time or is, say, within the gastric tract and not in its normal place, it changes colour and becomes black. So any blood that is within the gut, if it's fresh will be red, but if it has been around for some time, its chemical composition changes and it becomes very dark black.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: So an example from our everyday lives is, it's an inelegant word, but a scab on your knee when you fall over can go dark, can't it?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, it can go dark.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Is that the chemical process?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, in the gut it tends to be much more marked and should there be bleeding within the gut, by the time that altered blood comes out the other end in stool, the stool is often black and tarry. But if you -- because usually you don't have a nasogastric tube inside you, so you wouldn't be aspirating from the top end. But if blood was aspirated up, it would be black and tarry as well.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Okay. And how, in general terms, do premature babies of [Baby C]'s general presentation get altered blood in their stomachs?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Well, there are a number of ways really. Firstly, they have a nasogastric tube in situ and, depending on where the tip of that is, it can rub on the tummy. Also, [Baby C] wasn't fed, and therefore that's a stressful situation for a baby. He was also an unwell baby at the beginning of his life, which puts certain stresses on him. So that can cause some slight bleeding within the lining of the gut, which is usually trivial, so it's not uncommon to see altered blood. But also, it can be an effect of trauma. So there are a number of reasons.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: I just want to deal with things in chronological order rather than the reverse order you were just asked about.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Of course.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And starting with J1996, first of all, please. We're all familiar with this picture now. It was taken, as we can see, on 12 June.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: At 12.36 and 16 seconds; is that right?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: That shows the inflated stomach, as I understand it?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: So that was the position on the 12th.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I think you told the jury yesterday that you hadn't initially been able to see the -- I think you said the NGT; is that right?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: I think it's a matter of record, but at this stage it wasn't a nasogastric tube, was it?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: We know that he had an orogastric tube by the morning of the 13th, but I don't think the nursing record on the ITU chart actually says one way or the other what sort of tube is in.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Okay.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: But there is a gastric tube.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Yes. Just remind us, if this becomes important, why a baby this [Baby C]'s position would be given an oro, in other words through the mouth down the throat, gastric tube rather than a naso, ie through the nose, down the throat, gastric tube?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Of course he was very small, which we've already established, and therefore his nostrils were very small, and he was on CPAP, and that can be given by a little triangular mask, which seals over the nose and mouth or it can be given by prongs in the nostril. And in order to generate the pressure for CPAP, there has to be some sort of seal. So if he was receiving CPAP with nasal prongs, they have to fit very snugly within the nose.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And therefore in order -- because his nostril were so tiny, to have another tube in a nostril, ie a nasogastric tube, as well as these little prongs, would have distended his nostrils too much. So usually babies who are receiving nasal CPAP with a prong would have an orogastric tube in to prevent damage to the very delicate area around the nostril.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Are they called the nares?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, they are called the nares, yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: We heard some evidence about that, didn't we, and the nurse had put DuoDERM on [Baby C]'s nares?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, the blood supply between the nostrils is not very good and if you have continued pressure on that, the skin can actually break down. So you don't really want to have two tubes into one nostril because it can cause a problem.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Yes, okay. Just looking at the -- going back to the radiograph, please, which is on the screen. I think you told us that the end inside the body wasn't ideally placed in this picture; is that right?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: What effect would that placement of the end have on the decompression effect of what may well have been an oro rather than a nasogastric tube?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: The tip is only just in the stomach, so it only has just gone through the gullet into the stomach. So the only thing you can aspirate from there would be air, but you would have to -it wouldn't necessarily come out on its own, you'd have to aspirate it and record it. But the tube is very small, so you wouldn't actually get all the air out that way.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: For whatever reason, and we may come to this in a second, the tube is further out than it should be at this stage?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: So that's the position.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Can we go to J1922 next, please. This is Dr Ogden's note again. Okay?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: We see:
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: "Abdo soft, not distended."
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: And that stage, which we've already established, was 9.30 in the morning.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Is there a record in the note whether there was an oro or a nasogastric tube?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Not from Dr Ogden.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: So we move next to the nursing note, which was actually shown to you first, which is J1947. If you could magnify that, please. Thank you.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: So this is Nurse Williams', Joanne Williams', note, made at 16.38, I think, on the 13th. So this is 7 hours or so after Dr Ogden's notes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And 28 hours or so after the radiograph.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: I think it might have been completed at 16.38 and commenced at 16.19.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes. Thank you, my Lord. You're quite right.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Just looking at this note, this records that [Baby C] had had two orogastric tubes, doesn't it?
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, it does.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: What does it record, that he had -- and that's that morning, isn't it:
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: "Two OGTs this morning"?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: We heard evidence that he'd been pulling them out; do you remember that evidence?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, I do.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: If he'd been doing that at an earlier stage, would that account for the position of the tube on the radiograph taken on 12 June?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I don't think so because the nurses can tell if a baby is pulling a nasogastric tube out. It tends to be -- an orogastric tube in this case. It tends to be taped down. So if the baby gets their finger underneath it and pulls it out, it kinds of comes out in a loop.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: A nurse would notice that and therefore would not have allowed the X-ray to be undertaken with a kind of half-out tube.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: But that note does record, doesn't it, that the tube had been on free -- the tubes I should say, at least the nasogastric tube, sorry, because this is a point you made before, had been on free drainage?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes. I think the note is ambiguous. It just says that the nasogastric tube was on free drainage and that was only passed at 1 o'clock.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: All right. Thank you very much.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Does your Lordship have any questions?
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Questions from THE JUDGE
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Just in relation to your opinion that [Baby C] did not die from infection but died with infection. If a baby of his maturity, in other words very immature, and size dies of infection, what is the scenario of death generally? Is there a common scenario or not?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: It depends on where the infection is based, so whether it's a respiratory infection or meningitis or a urine infection. But usually, the baby would have a slow but continuous decline. So if it's a respiratory infection, you would expect him to require more oxygen, to be breathing more quickly and then need to go on to more invasive respiratory support, like a ventilator, then his heart would become affected, so he might need drugs to help his heart to pump. And all of that is an escalation of care required before effectively the baby would become unventilatable and you were not able to get oxygen into the baby despite intensive care measures, despite full
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: ventilation, despite a full amount of drugs to support the heart. If you still get poor blood gases and you can't oxygenate the baby, that's the way that the baby would then demise because you can no longer ventilate the baby. And obviously, none of -those things didn't happen.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: All right. I'm going to see if anyone wants to ask -- that did arise from the cross-examination, but if you want to ask any further questions, Mr Myers, in relation to that.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Of course.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Summary of interview with LUCY LETBY re [Baby C]
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: (read)
Ladies and gentlemen, Lucy Letby was interviewed about [Baby C]'s case on 4 July 2018.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: She said that she could remember [Baby C] because he was a small baby. She recalled that he, [Baby C], had deteriorated not long after his first ever feed by one of the nurses and said that she, Lucy Letby, had not been involved in that feed.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: She thought that Sophie Ellis, Dr Gibbs, Melanie Taylor and [Nurse B] were present at [Baby C]'s resuscitation and Lucy Letby said that her only involvement was with [Baby C]'s resuscitation, with which she had been asked to help.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Lucy Letby did not recall the events leading up to that and said that she was not aware of the circumstances of [Baby C]'s collapse. She said that [Baby C]'s designated nurse was Sophie Ellis, she couldn't remember to whom she, that is Lucy Letby, had been allocated, and she was not working in room 1 that night.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: She said that she could not recall having any care of [Baby C] other than his resuscitation, nor could she recall handling [Baby C] prior to resuscitation. She said that she had co-signed and/or checked the morphine that had been administered to [Baby C] after other treatment had been withdrawn and [Baby C]'s resuscitation was prolonged to enable a priest to attend and baptise him.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Lucy Letby said that she had a vague recollection of doing [Baby C]'s hand and footprints whilst [Baby C] was sat with his mum and dad, but could not be certain. She said she didn't know whether she had helped Sophie Ellis with that exercise.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: On 10 November 2020, when she was interviewed again, Lucy Letby was asked about the difficulties that had been experienced by Dr
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Davis in attempting to intubate [Baby C] and the swollen vocal cords that had been observed, and Lucy Letby denied having caused any injury to [Baby C]'s airway.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Lucy Letby said that she went to [Baby C] when he was with his mum and dad in the family room and that she would have had some interaction with them. She said she had found [Baby C]'s death quite hard because he lived for several hours after and she'd never seen that before.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Lucy Letby was asked about a conversation with [Baby C]'s parents in which one of the nurses had told them that they had said their goodbyes and asked if they wanted to place [Baby C] in a basket at a point before [Baby C] had passed away. She said she had no recollection of making that comment and questioned whether the parents were saying that she, Lucy Letby, was the nurse who had said that. She said that as far as she knew, she didn't say that comment to the parents and Lucy Letby commented that it was very sad for the parents.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Lucy Letby could not recall being told by [Nurse B] to stop helping Melanie Taylor in the aftermath of [Baby C]'s death and to go and look after her own designated baby. She said that the unit would usually pull together and try to support one another on something like that.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: She denied administering air to [Baby C] and she accepted that she had made Facebook searches for both [Mother of Baby C] and [Father of Baby C], which were approximately 10 hours after [Baby C] had died. She said she couldn't remember doing the search or why she would have done so.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Lucy Letby was asked about the series of WhatsApp messages between her and Jennifer Jones-Key on the evening of 13 June. She agreed that she'd wanted to go back into nursery 1 as it could be hard to go back into an intensive treatment unit environment after having had a sick baby, so she preferred to go straight back in.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: My Lord, that is the summary. Subject to the issues that we've just discussed relating to further expert evidence and putting the interview to one side, that is as far as we can take it with [Baby C]'s case at this stage.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Right. Thank you very much.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Well, as you will now have worked out, that's as far as we can go with the trial today. So you're getting an early day. Housekeeping
Yes, Mr Myers.

blocks.text: My Lord, we were most grateful this morning for the short delay before we could start. The situation, so far as Ms Letby is concerned, at the moment is as follows. For the past month or so there has been one team responsible for her transport and so undesirable, we suggest, though the situation has been, we have been able to work with that and done our best to do so.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: An important part of what takes place, given Ms Letby's condition, is the time at which she can arrive at court, speak with us, have something to eat and something to drink, be seen by the mental health support worker who has been involved with her, and that has been an enormous assistance, and it's important that I reiterate, as your Lordship is familiar with, that there are issues related to her ability to cope in an unsettled situation. I don't make more of it than that and I address that specifically to this stage of the proceedings. I recognise everything has to be considered on its merits according to the appropriate point of the proceedings. This is purely to do with how she's able to participate at the start of the day and at the conclusion of the day.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: The problem at the moment is that the team who had been transporting her appears to have changed. Those now responsible for this have a different organisation in terms of how they collect her. It's not the team's fault, this is the way the system is running. They are unable to collect as early as they could. It seems that --
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: As early as they have been?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: As early as they have been doing, I apologise.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: For whatever reason, the trip to court is taking a good deal longer. We understand it was about 2.5 hours today and then it would be 2.5 hours back at the end of the day -- it was about that yesterday -- which is a very long time for someone in these circumstances to be in a van like that before one even comes to the position of Ms Letby and the material the court has seen from all experts as to the potential effect of that in terms of transport.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: We will do what we can to communicate with the prison in the first instance to impress upon them the importance of a system being in place that allows for as smooth and swift a transit to and from court as possible. We recognise there are limits to what we and certainly the court, your Lordship, is able to do. But we identify the problem because it is one.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Given where we started or where we were at the beginning of this case, we, with the assistance of the court and all parties, and Ms Letby, have been in a position where we are able to deal with this without impediment and she is in as good a condition as could be expected for that. I don't mean any discourtesy to her when I talk about her like that, I'm sure she understands.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Our concern is, first of all, that it's not a suitable way of the day being run that there is a five-hour round trip with very minimal time at court for support, assistance and instructions. And that whilst in the immediate moment that is unhelpful, the long-term consequences of an arrangement like that upon her will be detrimental.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: So we are anxious to try to see if steps can be taken to improve this method of transport so it is swifter and smoother.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Yes. Do you know whether what's happened today is going to be the pattern for the future or not or is this just a one-off? I don't know whether anyone who's with the defendant is able to assist in relation to this.

blocks.text: Our understanding, if I can hand over to the prison officer in a moment, is there are two issues.
